lessons.title: The speaking test, explained
lessons.summary: Learn what happens in Parts 1, 2 and 3.
lessons.body: The speaking test has three parts. Part 1 covers familiar questions. In Part 2 you prepare for one minute, then speak for up to two minutes. Part 3 develops more abstract ideas related to the cue card. Practise moving from a personal answer to a wider discussion.
lessons.task: Try answering “What do you enjoy about where you live?” Then explain how cities could become better places to live.

lessons.title: Turn a short answer into a story
lessons.body: Start with a direct answer. Explain why you feel that way. Add a real example, then finish with a short reflection. You do not need to force all four steps into every Part 1 answer. Keep each detail relevant.
lessons.task: Instead of “I like reading”, try “I enjoy reading because it helps me unwind. Last week I finished a mystery novel on my commute.”

lessons.title: Find your natural flow
lessons.body: Speak for 45 seconds about a familiar activity. When you need a moment, pause naturally. Avoid restarting an entire sentence for a small mistake. Review one recording and notice where an unfinished thought made your meaning unclear.
lessons.task: Describe your morning routine. Repeat the task, keeping your main ideas but reducing unnecessary restarts.

lessons.title: Grammar you can actually use
lessons.summary: Build accurate sentences, one pattern at a time.
lessons.body: Use the present perfect continuous for something that began in the past and is still happening. “I have been living here for five years.” Use “for” with a duration and “since” with a starting point. A natural contraction is “I’ve been living here…”
lessons.task: Say how long you have been studying English. Then say when you started.

lessons.title: Vocabulary that sounds like you
lessons.summary: Choose accurate expressions over difficult words.
lessons.body: Simple language can be excellent language. Replace vague words when a more precise expression fits your meaning. “A lively neighbourhood” tells us more than “a very good place”. Do not add idioms just to sound advanced.
lessons.task: Describe your hometown using “lively”, “convenient” or “peaceful”, only if the word matches your experience.

lessons.title: Paraphrase without losing meaning
lessons.summary: Express the same idea in more than one way.
lessons.body: Paraphrasing is flexible expression, not word-for-word substitution. “I like spending time outdoors” can become “I enjoy being outside”. Some words naturally go together, such as “make a decision” and “gain experience”.
lessons.task: Give two natural ways to say “I like learning new things”.

lessons.title: Make your meaning easy to follow
lessons.summary: Connect ideas with a clear purpose.
lessons.body: Use connections that match your ideas: “because” for a reason, “for example” for an illustration, and “although” for a contrast. A long list of linking phrases does not automatically make an answer coherent.
lessons.task: Explain a preference, give a reason, then mention one drawback.

lessons.title: Build a two-minute cue-card answer
lessons.body: Write a few keywords for each cue point, not a script. Build your answer around a specific event or experience. Cover the important points, then develop why the experience mattered to you.
lessons.task: Choose a memorable journey. Note where, when, who and why, then record an answer.

lessons.title: Discuss ideas with confidence
lessons.summary: Consider causes, effects and alternative views.
lessons.body: State a view, explain your reasoning and support it with an example. If the issue has more than one side, acknowledge a reasonable alternative. Avoid presenting every personal opinion as an established fact.
lessons.task: Should cities invest more in public transport? Give one advantage and one challenge.

lessons.title: Be understood clearly
lessons.summary: Focus on intelligibility, stress and rhythm.
lessons.body: You do not need to imitate a particular accent. Group words into meaningful phrases and stress important words. Record a short sentence and listen for sounds or word boundaries that make your message hard to understand.
lessons.task: Say “One of the main reasons is convenience.” Stress “main reasons” and “convenience”.

lessons.title: Finish the thought
lessons.body: A spoken answer can contain short phrases naturally. A problem occurs when the listener cannot understand your intended meaning. After recording, find any sentence where you started an explanation but never completed it.
lessons.task: Complete this idea in your own words: “The main thing I would change about my city is…”

lessons.title: Review, retry, remember
lessons.summary: Turn feedback into a useful habit.
lessons.body: Choose one correction. Understand why it matters, then answer the same question again without reading a model answer. Compare the attempts. Keep corrections available even after you mark them reviewed.
lessons.task: Practise one saved grammar correction in three new sentences.

lessons.title: Part 1: personal and specific
lessons.summary: Give a clear answer with a useful detail.
lessons.body: Respond directly to the question. Add a brief reason or a real detail. Avoid memorised introductions and long speeches for a simple personal question.
lessons.task: Answer “Do you enjoy cooking?” in two or three natural sentences.

lessons.title: Pause with purpose
lessons.body: A brief pause is natural. Excessive filler and repeated restarts can make an answer harder to follow. Try pausing at the end of a thought rather than halfway through a phrase.
lessons.task: Speak for 30 seconds about your weekend and listen for repeated fillers.

lessons.title: Stress and intonation
lessons.summary: Use your voice to support your meaning.
lessons.body: Content words often carry stress. Intonation can show whether you have finished a thought, are asking a question, or are expressing uncertainty. Listen to your recording and notice whether your phrasing helps the listener.
lessons.task: Read the same sentence once as a statement and once as a surprised question.

lessons.title: Speak with more flexibility
lessons.body: Qualify broad claims when appropriate: “in some cases”, “often” and “it depends on…” can make your meaning more accurate. Use examples to explain nuance, rather than adding complexity for its own sake.
lessons.task: Discuss whether working from home suits everyone. Consider two different types of worker.
